HEADLINE: 'Day of shame,' says association boss
TEXT:
The banking industry has candidly admitted the damning findings in the financial services commission's interim report are a "day of shame" for financial institutions.

Commissioner Kenneth Hayne's blistering report published Friday blamed a culture of greed and institutions putting short-term profits before people for endemic customer rip-offs across banks, financial planners, insurers and superannuation funds.

He also blamed the corporate regulator for being too soft on the financial sector and suggested it better enforce existing laws.

Australian Banking Association chief executive Anna Bligh said the report's findings were "shocking" and that banks must work hard to win back the trust of the community.

"Our banks have failed in many ways. Failed customers, failed to obey the law and failed to meet community standards," she said. "Too many customers have been hurt and it has to stop.

"Make no mistake. Today is a day of shame for Australia's banks."

Despite the mea culpa and scathing assessment in Mr Hayne's near-1000 page report, the big banks' shares rallied.

The report did not make firm recommendations, instead asking a series of questions about enforcing the law better and whether rules should be simplified.

ANZ boss Shayne Elliott said: "This is a critical moment for the industry, our bank and our people to continue the urgent work required to fix the significant failures highlighted by the commission. We accept responsibility and we are determined to improve."

Commonwealth Bank of Australia chief Matt Comyn said the interim report was confronting. "We have seen too many examples of unacceptable behaviour and unacceptable customer outcomes," he said in a statement.

"The commission has highlighted the need for significant changes, particularly to systems, processes and culture. I am committed to making sure that we learn from the failures detailed in this report to fix what went wrong and put things right for our customers."

"We will provide a comprehensive response to the interim report."

National Australia Bank chief executive Andrew Thorburn said he had read a summary of the report and would review it in more detail at the weekend.

"For us at NAB, where we have made mistakes or done the wrong thing, we will own them and fix them. It is difficult to face the statement of 'profits before people', but this is exactly what we need to confront."

The Consumer Action Law Centre and Financial Rights Legal Centre said in a joint statement it was clear the finance sector can't be trusted to self-regulate. "The lack of consequences for banks and lenders for misconduct is driving poor lending and sales practices that are hurting Australians who can least afford it. Where loans are found to be irresponsibly lent, debts should be waived - this will provide the right incentive for banks to do the right thing," said Consumer Action Law Centre chief Gerard Brody.

"The government must act to fix our broken banks and properly resource our regulators so that they can hold the industry to account for misconduct."

Financial Sector Union national secretary Julia Angrisano said the commission's hearings had revealed appalling stories of corporate greed and a disturbing lack of compassion for customers. She called for better governance, regulation and culture.

Westpac chief Brian Hartzer said the commission had identified many examples of misconduct across the industry.

"I apologise to any customers who have been impacted by mistakes that we have made," he said.

"While we've introduced a number of reforms, including to our remuneration structures, our approaches to dealing with customer issues and removing grandfathered commissions attributable to BT products, we know we still have more work to do."

The profits of financial institutions are already being hurt by the commission. They are spending hundreds of millions of dollars on lawyers and compensating customers.

Westpac on Thursday announced its cash earnings would be cut by $235 million, or about 3 per cent of earnings per share, as it undertakes further work to address customer issues and provisions for litigation. The increase in provisions were for financial planning fee-for-no-advice violations and refunds for inadequate financial advice.

UBS bank analysts say more provisions by banks are likely.

HEADLINE: Regulator failure in its cosiness with the banks
TEXT:
The greed exposed by the banking royal commission has largely been laid at the feet of the corporate regulator for being too cosy with the banks and failing to take them to court.

Commissioner Kenneth Hayne found that when misconduct was revealed, it largely "went unpunished" as the Australian Securities and Investments Commission sought to negotiate, rather than litigate a penalty.

Treasurer Josh Frydenberg doubled down on the criticism at a news conference on Friday where he said it was ASIC's culture, rather than a lack of powers or funding that let offenders off the hook.

"This is clearly unacceptable and cannot continue," Mr Frydenberg said. "The findings here go to a culture of negotiation rather litigation. Too often the regulator would seek a negotiated outcome rather than take the next step to litigate and make them face court. Perpetrators got off too lightly."

ASIC's enforcement record laid bare by Commissioner Hayne makes for brutal reading. It paves the way for a return to the big litigation approach of former ASIC chairman Tony D'Aloisio, who brought major cases against James Hardie, Centro, Fortescue and AWB, with mixed results.

In the decade to June 1 this year, ASIC's infringement notices to the major banks amounted to less than $1.3 million while CBA declared a profit 7000 times greater ($9.93 billion last year).

Commissioner Hayne singled out a $180,000 fine to Commonwealth Bank for breaching consumer credit provisions after a computer error meant for four years the bank failed to take account of customers' living expenses when calculating their ability to service the loan.

There also was evidence of CBA making a $300,000 donation over a CommInsure advertisement rather than facing an $8 million fine and toning down the media release issued by ASIC.

More than half ASIC's 1102 proceedings over the past decade have been administrative and, of the others, just 10 were against the major banks with most of those out of Storm Financial and the bank bill swap rate cases, the report said.

Before the hearings, ASIC had not begun civil penalty proceedings against a financial adviser in the past five years.

The report said the commission was considering an individual licensing system for financial advisers similar to doctors and lawyers, so that dodgy advisers no longer could fly under the radar by flocking to "licensees of last resort".

The interim report found "ASIC rarely went to court to seek public denunciation of and punishment for misconduct".

"Little happened beyond apology from the entity, a drawn-out remediation program and protracted negotiation with ASIC of a media release, an infringement notice, or an enforceable undertaking that acknowledged no more than that ASIC had reasonable 'concerns' about the entity's conduct," the interim report says.

"Infringement notices imposed penalties that were immaterial for the large banks. Enforceable undertakings might require a 'community benefit payment', but the amount was far less than the penalty that ASIC could properly have asked a court to impose."

While ASIC shoulders most of the blame, the report also takes aim at the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority for lack of an enforcement culture. "The prudential regulator, APRA, never went to court," the report says.

ASIC chairman James Shipton, who started in the role after being appointed by the government this year, "welcomed" the report and said it would respond in full in its submission by October 26.

Mr Frydenberg was asked why the regulator fell into the trap of negotiating penalties with the banks in an approach Commissioner Hayne has found failed badly. "I think it was a strategy that they had which saw the regulator working too closely with the sector they are regulating," he said.

HEADLINE: Heavier punishment for greedy banks
TEXT:
Regulators are in for a major shake-up after royal commissioner Kenneth Hayne found the culture of greed permeating the financial services sector was a result of a failure to follow and enforce existing rules.

The commissioner's interim report castigated the nation's banks for repeatedly and systematically crossing the line in the pursuit of profits in a scorching assessment of our financial system and its key players. "The banks have gone to the edge of what is permitted, and too often beyond that limit, in pursuit of profit," the report, which was released yesterday, said.

But bank shares immediately rallied on the commissioner's suggestion that more regulation was not the answer.

Commissioner Hayne zeroed in on the contribution of feckless regulators, a lack of competition and the conflict created through the ownership of bank shares by superannuation funds as key to understanding how this has been allowed to happen, and why it has gone on for so long. The report focuses on the motivations of the bankers in the opening pages.

"Too often the answer seems to be greed - the pursuit of short-term profit at the expense of basic standards of honesty. How else is charging continuing advice fees to the dead to be explained?" it said.

The commissioner highlighted the pursuit of profits and monetary gain on the part of the banks and regulators that preferred negotiated outcomes over the enforcement of the law.

The egregious behaviour from the wealth management sector and financial intermediaries such as mortgage brokers was sheeted directly back to remuneration. "For individuals, the conduct resulted in being paid more. For entities, the conduct resulted in greater profit," the report said.

Hayne equated misconduct by bankers with bigger bonuses and greater profits, crucially asking how a value-based commission would ever be in the best interests of a client.

"How is a value-based commission consistent with acting in the interests, or best interests, of the client?"

In other findings, Commissioner Hayne said that AMP executives had persistently dealt with the regulator ASIC in an underhanded manner but he did not make findings, at this stage, on the conduct of former chair Catherine Brenner, former CEO Craig Meller and former group general counsel Brian Salter, who all left the company after the commission's hearings. He also found that CBA's risk-control systems for personal overdrafts were utterly inadequate and that NAB failed to provide mortgage services efficiently, honestly and fairly.

The 1000-page report has stopped short of making recommendations and, instead, asked if what was needed was better enforcement of the law and a simplification of current laws to aid those who enforce it.

"Much more often than not, the conduct now condemned was contrary to law. Passing some new law to say, again, 'Do not do that', would add an extra layer of legal complexity to an already complex regulatory regime. What would that gain?" the report reads.

While the banks were heavily criticised, Commissioner Hayne also made it clear plenty of fault lies with the regulator, describing fines handed out to the banks which make tens of billions in profit each year as "immaterial".

"When misconduct was revealed, it either went unpunished or the consequences did not meet the seriousness of what had been done," the report said.

While the report contained no recommendations, the financial services industry is bracing for the removal of grandfathering arrangements which see financial advisers reap millions in commissions each year with Commissioner Hayne effectively putting the final nail in the coffin with three questions.

"Should the grandfathered exceptions to the conflicted remuneration provisions now be changed? - How far should they be changed? - If they should be changed, when should the change or changes take effect?" the report asks.

Bank shares rallied on the release of the report - taking comfort from the lack of recommendations - posting gains three to four times that of the broader market.

ANZ rose 1.4 per cent, CBA rose 1.9 per cent, NAB rose 1.8 per cent and Westpac rose 1.2 per cent compared with the 0.4 per cent gain from the ASX 200.

Treasurer Josh Frydenberg said the industry needed to lift its game and the actions of the regulators were unacceptable. "The two key take-outs for me have been that greed has permeated the culture, the compliance of the sector and, secondly, the misconduct has gone to a large degree unpunished," the Treasurer said.

When pressed on the role of the regulator he said, "I think it shows they need to be tougher" and said the issues at the regulator were "deeper" than needing additional resources.

Federal Labor seized on the interim report to criticise Prime Minister Scott Morrison for trying so hard for so long to stop a royal commission.

"This is the report that Scott Morrison never wanted," acting Opposition leader Tanya Plibersek said.

Labor moved again to get ahead of the Coalition on the issue by promising that, if elected next year, it would establish a financial services royal commission implementation task force "to reform the culture of profit over people".

A spokesman for the government said plans for a similar body were under way and it had already started recruiting for key roles.

Commissioner Hayne was scathing of ASIC in the report, saying the problem was not so much the rules outlawing bad behaviour, but the lack of enforcement and the light penalties handed out.

"The conduct regulator, ASIC, rarely went to court to seek public denunciation of and punishment for misconduct. The prudential regulator, APRA, never went to court," the report said.

A willingness to negotiate cannot be the starting point for the regulator, the report said. "A regulator 'speaking softly' will rarely be effective unless the regulator also carries a big stick."

Commissioner Hayne hinted that ASIC may need to be restructured because its remit was too big and its culture of negotiating outcomes rather than handing out punishment was too entrenched.

ASIC chairman James Shipton issued a short statement about the report, noting the "serious and important observations of ASIC's role as a regulator" and promising to continue assisting the inquiry.

Commissioner Hayne identifies the lack of competition in the Australian banking sector alongside the large holdings of bank shares by super funds as key reasons for understanding not only what has happened but why it was allowed to continue.

HEADLINE: Fleet Labor opens fire on Morrison
TEXT:
Ever since Scott Morrison replaced Malcolm Turnbull, Labor has been struggling to find the right line and length with the new Prime Minister.

That appeared to change with Friday's release of Commissioner Kenneth Hayne's interim report, which acting Labor leader Tanya Plibersek quickly badged as "the report that Scott Morrison never wanted".

"The Liberals have never taken this seriously. They were dragged kicking and screaming into holding a royal commission and they gave it an unreasonably short time frame."

Hours before the report was tabled, Labor released a 45-second commercial titled "Scott Morrison, whose side are you really on?", which detailed the myriad excuses Morrison, as Treasurer, gave over the months as he fought a royal commission. These included "populist whinge", "reckless distraction", "opportunistic" and "let's not forget that our banking and finance sector is a well regulated sector".

In recent weeks, Morrison has twice conceded openly that he was wrong to have opposed the commission.

He admitted he was preoccupied with trying to fix the problem with rules and regulations while being oblivious to the hurt the industry had inflicted on people, their right to be heard, and the need to effect cultural change by publicly shaming the villains.

He should be given a pat on the back for admitting fault. It is rare these days. Ultimately, however, the only reason the government caved in and called the royal commission was because it faced being rolled by its own backbench.

Labor is entitled to press home what it senses is a clear advantage.

More so after Commissioner Hayne, in his refreshingly simple and honest style, effectively concluded it wasn't a lack of rules and regulation that was the problem, it was that nobody followed or enforced the existing rules.

"I begin from the premise that breaches of existing law are not prevented by passing some new law that says 'Do not do that'," he says.

"When misconduct was revealed, it either went unpunished or the consequences did not meet the seriousness of what had been done."

One could argue that the government, as it piled red tape on red tape to try to ward off the royal commission, had been wasting everybody's time.

Treasurer Josh Frydenberg has obviously been sniffing the breeze in recent weeks and announced a fortnight ago that ASIC had been a failure in the past and would be given greater powers, including those of remediation.

On Friday, he left open the prospect of greater structural reform after Hayne suggested ASIC may need to be restructured because its remit was too big and its culture of negotiating outcomes (appeasement) rather than handing out punishment, was too entrenched.

Still, it was Labor that was fleet of foot on the day. Plibersek promised that Labor, if elected next year, would establish a financial services royal commission implementation taskforce to ensure Hayne's recommendations were swiftly delivered.

Hayne's final report is due by February 1, less than three months before the election. His initial findings should stymie any pre-election arms race between the major parties.

HEADLINE: Brutal interim volley but little action
TEXT:
The sheer brutality of Commissioner Kenneth Hayne's interim report is what hits you first. Hayne might be known as a black-letter lawyer, but he does not hide behind legalese to explain the myriad of examples of misconduct he has seen in the first four rounds of the hearings.

"Too often, the answer seems to be greed - the pursuit of short-term profit at the expense of basic standards of honesty. How else is charging continuing advice fees to the dead to be explained?" Hayne asks.

"Banks, and all financial services entities, recognised that they sold services and products. Selling became their focus of attention. Too often it became the sole focus of attention."

This is a description of an industry that has become blinkered and arrogant, pursuing profit above all else.

But those seeking a list of urgent actions that the government needs to take to address these issues will be disappointed. The solutions that the community so badly deserves are not delivered in this interim report.

Indeed, Hayne has chosen to structure the document as a set of observations and further questions that he will seek to answer in his final report. This two-step process was clearly always Hayne's intention.

But so clear were many of the examples of misconduct, and so urgent the fixes to problems uncovered in the commission, that it is somewhat surprising Hayne hasn't given the government direction on the sort of areas it should start to focus on.

A list of examples of misconduct that ASIC should begin to chase now might have also been a reasonable first step.

No wonder bank share prices jumped following the publication of the report. If the banks will be hanging their collective heads in shame at this ugly summation of their industry - and they should - then it is the regulators that surely take the brunt of Hayne's initial observations.

The Australian Securities and Investment Commission is lashed for its enforcement approach, and complete unwillingness to go after the banks and institutions with the full force of the laws under which it works.

The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority fares little better.

"The conduct regulator, ASIC, rarely went to court to seek public denunciation of and punishment for misconduct. The prudential regulator, APRA, never went to court," Hayne says. "Much more often than not, when misconduct was revealed, little happened beyond apology from the entity, a drawn-out remediation program and protracted negotiation with ASIC of a media release, an infringement notice, or an enforceable undertaking that acknowledged no more than that ASIC had reasonable 'concerns' about the entity's conduct.

"Too often, entities have been treated in ways that would allow them to think that they, not ASIC, not the Parliament, not the courts, will decide when and how the law will be obeyed or the consequences of breach remedied."

Hayne sets out many questions that he will need to address in order to address the issues he has exposed. But that's not to say that we can't get a flavour of the changes Hayne might eventually recommend.

See this on responsible lending, for example: "Lending was treated as not unsuitable if the customer was unlikely to default. But that is not what the responsible lending provisions required. Contrary to those provisions, the banks made no inquiry about the customer's circumstances, requirements or objectives."

Or see this on grandfathered commission in wealth management: "If the premise for the conflicted remuneration provisions is accepted (and no one suggested that it should not be), how can the grandfathering provisions be justified today?"

Or this on ongoing service agreements, where clients were charged fees but not provided with the promised services: "Advisers often treated ongoing service arrangements as though they were nothing but trail commissions for the advice that had already been given."

But Hayne cautions on the approach to new legal measures. He argues that simply "passing some new law to say, again, 'Do not do that', would add an extra layer of legal complexity to an already complex regulatory regime" and would be ineffective.

His push is to simplify the law by setting six clear, simple tenets for banks to follow: Obey the law; do not mislead or deceive; be fair; provide services that are fit for purpose; deliver services with reasonable care and skill; and, when acting for another, act in the best interests of that other.

"These ideas are very simple. Their simplicity points firmly towards a need to simplify the existing law rather than add some new layer of regulation," Hayne says.

"But the more complicated the law, the easier it is to lose sight of them. The more complicated the law, the easier it is for compliance to be seen as asking 'Can I do this?' and answering that question by ticking boxes instead of asking 'Should I do this? What is the right thing to do?"'

It's a good theory. But it's worth pointing out the current legislative framework has some simple ideas in it too, like acting at all times in the "best interests" of customers.

Hayne's report suggests the banks appear to have largely failed to understand even this simple idea.

The regulators ... surely take the brunt of Hayne's initial observations.

HEADLINE: Get set for a banker pay revolution
TEXT:
Australia's biggest banks and insurers have been bracing themselves for a blistering denunciation from the royal commission's interim report.

But they have also been consoling themselves with the idea that, once all the furore died down, life was likely to continue pretty much as it had in the halcyon pre-commission days.

In other words, they completely underestimated the formidable intelligence, and intellectual courage, that Commissioner Kenneth Hayne would demonstrate as he grappled with the two key questions arising from his inquiry: what has led to such widespread misbehaviour by bankers, financial planners and insurers, and what should be done about it?

Like many before him, Hayne was quick to identify an overwhelming motivation: greed.

As he argues in the royal commission interim report, "the conduct identified and criticised in this report was driven by the pursuit of profit - the entity's revenue and profit and the individual actor's profit. Employees of banks learned to treat sales, or revenue and profit, as the measure of their success."

But even the dimmest banker realised that the industry's remuneration practices were going to come in for particular scrutiny by the Hayne royal commission. And so, with various degrees of enthusiasm, banks have been moving to realign their pay structures, so that employees were rewarded for intangible factors such as adhering to proper behavioural standards as well as for the profit they generated. As a result, bankers appearing before the commission were able to boast that they were using a more enlightened "balanced scorecard" approach for rewarding their staff.

But Hayne is unconvinced this modest rejig of the method for calculating bankers' salaries will produce the desired improvement in standards. "The banks say that they have changed or are changing their remuneration policies and it will be necessary to look carefully at those claims."

But, worryingly for the banking fraternity, Hayne's scepticism runs much, much deeper. He's profoundly dubious about the pay structure that banks use for rewarding all their employees - from the most senior executives to the most junior employees. This remuneration structure has two parts: a base salary, and then a short-term incentive payment or bonus.

Now, Hayne is bemused by the fact that frequently, bank employees receive their bonuses even if their performance is only satisfactory, and they've merely done what they've been employed to do. As Hayne notes, "The premise must be that the immediate supervisor either cannot, or will not, adequately manage and supervise those employees."

More importantly, Hayne notes that profit retains its central position, even in the "balanced scorecard" approach. That's because employees are keenly aware of what their employers regard as most important.

"When the employee and others in the organisation, included the employee's supervisors and peers, are remunerated according to how much product they sell, or how much revenue or profit they contribute to the entity, sales or revenue and profit are treated as the goal to pursue."

Indeed, the report notes that using behavioural standards along with sales performance to calculate bonuses can potentially encourage dissembling by employees. "If the short-term incentive scheme reduces the amount allowed if an employee does not meet some standard (of accuracy, or behaviour) the employee may focus as much upon avoiding error being discovered as upon avoidance of error."

But this leads Hayne to query whether a much more radical overhaul of bank remuneration practices should be considered - one that stretches from the most junior bank tellers to the very pinnacle of those worthy institutions.

As Hayne puts it, "the unstated premise" in the whole debate about paying bank employees bonuses - that is, that they won't do their job properly and to the best of their ability unless they get incentives - needs challenge.

Hayne, however, isn't just asking if junior staff should stop being given incentive payments. Rewarding senior executives with bonuses based on lifting profits will reverberate through the organisation.

In other words, improving the culture of Australian banks will involve a radical shake-up of their entrenched approach to rewarding staff, from the chief executive down.

"Why will altering the remuneration of front-line staff effect a change in culture if more senior employees are rewarded for sales or revenue and profit?" Hayne asks.

Little wonder that the commissioner notes that this process "may not be easy and may take time".

HEADLINE: Grandfathering regime set to be shown the door
TEXT:
Grandfathered commissions are on borrowed time after banking royal commissioner Kenneth Hayne rejected the reasons put forward by banks for keeping the conflicted pay structures.

Commissioner Hayne says although some companies have resisted moves to abolish grandfathering by asking what evidence exists to support taking such a drastic step, the proper question is, "Why should the grandfathering provisions remain?"

The Future of Financial Advice laws, which took hold in 2013, banned conflicted remuneration. But agreements with clients entered into before that time were allowed to continue; they were "grandfathered".

The corporate regulator told the commission that while grandfathering remains, there is a "risk of misaligned incentives, which can lead to inappropriate advice".

Since the hearings Westpac, Macquarie, NAB and ANZ have all announced they will cease paying grandfathered commissions to the advisers they employ, although a big question mark remains over commissions for non-salaried advisers.

AMP, which derives 20 per cent of its financial advice revenue from trailing commissions, has resisted.

"AMP submitted that the grandfathering arrangements provided for in the Fofa arrangements should remain in place and, in effect, should over time be allowed to wither on the vine," Commissioner Hayne's interim report says.

He says AMP also alluded to the prospect that such a change may constitute acquisition of property on something other than just terms.

But the experienced legal practitioner is sceptical.

"First, where would be the 'acquisition'? Who would acquire anything? It is not apparent that any proprietary benefit or interest would accrue to any person."

Company executives also sought to convince the commission that other barriers to abolishing grandfathering exist, including immutable contracts with advisers and the idea that reducing commission income would ultimately hurt consumers because they would pay more for advice.

Yet since the hearings, and five years on from Fofa's inception, there is movement on the grandfathering front.

Westpac, Macquarie, NAB and ANZ have announced abolition plans.

The royal commission heard that the old commission-type arrangements had in some cases been replaced with "ongoing service fees".

These had also proved problematic because they led to similarly conflicted decision-making.

Both the Australian Securities and Investments Commission and Treasury have indicated support for an end to grandfathered commissions.

Neither of the major parties has proposed such a move but South Australian senator Rex Patrick is preparing a draft bill that would phase out commissions by mid-2020.

The royal commission heard evidence about Commonwealth Financial Planning, which continues to receive grandfathered commissions.

HEADLINE: AMP may have misled ASIC on amended Clayton Utz report
TEXT:
Royal commissioner Kenneth Hayne has found AMP may have made false representations about the independence of a controversial report prepared by law firm Clayton Utz that was at the centre of the resignation of former chairman Catherine Brenner.

While commissioner Hayne did not make any finding about the misconduct of Ms Brenner or former chief executive Craig Meller in relation to the report, he said it "may be open to conclude that AMP knew that the report was not an independent report".

"Conduct of that kind, if established, might be misconduct," Mr Hayne said in his interim report, released on Friday. "I consider that AMP may have made false representations to ASIC about the character of the Clayton Utz report."

AMP commissioned the report from Clayton Utz in June 2017, asking the firm to look into the group's controversial buyer of last resort (BOLR) policy, which required AMP to buy an agent's book of clients when the agent was leaving the industry.

The exercise of the clause saw many clients tipped into a customer pool where some fees were charged for services not provided.

AMP presented the report to the Australian Securities and Investment Commission in a meeting on October 16, 2017, having described the report as the result of an "independent investigation" by Clayton Utz. But as evidence presented to the commission showed, the report had been the subject of series of drafts - Commissioner Hayne put it at 22 - after changes and amendments suggested by AMP and particularly its former chief legal counsel, Brian Salter.

"AMP sent numerous emails to Clayton Utz with marked up drafts or suggested amendments to the draft," commissioner Hayne said.

"The amendments proposed appear on their face to suggest alterations to what findings were made in the report about the extent of the knowledge and involvement of particular executives of AMP in the impugned ongoing service fee conduct.

In one particular change, the law firm was asked by AMP to "include a statement to the effect that ... Mr Meller ... was unaware" of the practices around the mischarging of the BOLR clients, or the illegality of those practices.

Ms Brenner resigned on April 30, just 10 days after Mr Meller's departure from the group was brought forward in the wake of the commission's round of hearings on the wealth industry. AMP denied any wrongdoing in relation to the report.

However, Commissioner Hayne said "having regard to the number and nature of the changes made to drafts of the report ... it may be open to find that AMP implicitly or explicitly misled ASIC as to the character of the Clayton Utz report" in that the wealth giant represented the report as "external and independent".

But he said, "having not heard evidence from Ms Brenner, Mr Meller, Mr Salter, or from any partner of Clayton Utz, I make no findings about their conduct".

Commissioner Hayne also questioned AMP's defence over the Clayton Utz report, suggesting that the AMP board had expressed its surprise at the number of interventions in the report by Mr Salter "while at the same time ... asserting that Mr Salter's numerous interventions in the drafting process were not untoward".

The report said it is "not at all easy to understand why so many employees and executives at AMP were unable to recognise that to charge fees for services that will not, and cannot, be provided is not just unlawful, but also ethically and morally wrong".

AMP said it was reviewing the interim report but it wants to "help restore the community's trust and confidence in our company and the industry".

"We are accelerating remediation to ensure affected customers are appropriately compensated as quickly as possible," acting chief executive Mike Wilkins said.

AMP shares rose 1.6 per cent to $3.19 on Friday.

HEADLINE: Guarantors
TEXT:
Carolyn Flanagan,

disability pensioner

"I'd have signed anything for her, love. If you can't help your children, who can you help?"

The terminally ill woman, stricken by cancer and survivor of multiple strokes, lost her home to Westpac after acting as guarantor for her daughter's business. Westpac at first rejected a settlement that would allow her to stay in the home until she died."

What Hayne says | "I cannot say from the material presented in evidence whether the guarantee may have been unenforceable.

"Once Ms Flanagan made her hardship application, I consider that the community would not think it right for Westpac to deprive Ms Flanagan of the use of her home during her life. And yet, despite her expressed desire to negotiate what would be, in effect, a life tenancy in the property, Westpac rebuffed the approach. That was conduct that fell short of what the community would expect."
